title: Android Bench 2 Adds Support for Long-Horizon Tasks, Agentic Evaluation, and Continuous Scoring
gist: Google's Android Bench 2.0 adds multi-day long-horizon tasks, agentic evaluation and continuous scoring; Claude Opus 5.5 leads with a 32% LHT pass rate ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 28%, and results show AI is stronger at new code and deterministic transformations than refactoring or cross-platform porting.

insights.claim: On Android Bench 2.0, Claude Opus 5.5 led with a 32% long-horizon-task pass rate, followed by GPT 6 Astra at 28%.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Anthropic holds a narrow lead on agentic coding benchmarks over OpenAI; low absolute rates show headroom.
insights.quote: Claude Opus 5.5 was at the top of the leaderboard with a 32% LHT pass rate, followed by GPT 6 Astra at 28%.

insights.claim: The Android Bench 2.0 dashboard includes Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, OpenAI GPT-6, Anthropic Fable 5.1, Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 Max, with agents evaluated from corresponding model providers.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Chinese models (Kimi, Qwen) are benchmarked alongside US frontier labs on agentic coding.

themes.theme: Benchmark design shift to long-horizon agents

insights.claim: Android Bench 2.0 introduces long-horizon tasks that take an engineer multiple days or a week, such as dependency upgrades, new features, building apps from scratch, or converting cross-platform apps to Android.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Benchmarks are moving to multi-day agentic work, the frontier relevant to AI coding monetization.

insights.claim: Android Bench moved from binary pass/fail to continuous completion scoring based on functionality, visual fidelity and avoiding regressions, with penalties for deviating from instructions.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Partial-credit scoring better reflects real economic value of imperfect agent output.

themes.theme: Where AI coding works and fails

insights.claim: Google reports that AI does a better job writing new code than refactoring existing code, because refactoring and migrations require understanding architectural complexity.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Brownfield modernization remains harder to automate than greenfield, affecting AI code modernization vendor claims.
insights.quote: AI does a better job at writing new code rather than refactoring existing code
insights.locator: The results provided by Android Bench 2.0

insights.claim: AI performs well on well-established deterministic transformations even in larger codebases, such as Java to Kotlin, Retrofit to Ktor, or introducing a ViewModel layer.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Mechanical migrations are the near-term sweet spot for AI coding agents.

insights.claim: Models still struggle with tasks requiring runtime validation, breaking framework changes, or unreleased libraries; the best model reaches only 80% completion porting a cross-platform app to Android, an 'open challenge'.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Identifies concrete capability gaps limiting full autonomy of coding agents.
